{"body": "I am asked to develop an account of the black-hole information problem, but I am working from a node whose only selected prior view is a placeholder that says, in effect, that no earlier source was supplied. I therefore have no earlier formulation in front of me to operate on, and I will not pretend that I do. What I can do is state the problem carefully, note the structural pieces that any solution must address, and flag where the view I actually have is too thin to support a verdict.

The question, as posed, is not merely 'what does a distant observer see?' It is: if matter in a definite physical state collapses into a black hole, and the hole later evaporates completely into outgoing radiation, what happens to the information that distinguished that initial state? Several distinct concerns are often bundled here. One is unitary evolution: the standard quantum formalism evolves pure states to pure states under a unitary map, so a pure initial state should remain pure. A second is the species and entanglement structure of Hawking radiation: a semiclassical calculation gives a thermal-looking flux whose entropy appears to rise, apparently at odds with a globally pure final state. A third is the status of the interior: if the interior degrees of freedom that carry the infalling information are gone, where is the information? A fourth is whether 'information' here means the full microstate, the coarse-grained macroscopic state, or something operational about reconstructing correlations.

Without an earlier body, I cannot attribute a position to the prior node on any of these. I can still say what constraints seem fairly robust and where they collide. Robust: semiclassical field theory on a fixed or slowly evolving background produces radiation that is extremely close to thermal for an old black hole, so any account must reproduce that near-thermal appearance. Robust: if the process is unitary, the fine-grained entropy of the radiation must eventually fall, and correlations must exist that a semiclassical calculation does not track. Robust: local effective field theory in a single exterior region is very successful, so any proposal that changes it must explain why it looked right. Contentious: whether unitarity is preserved at all, whether a remnant, a firewall, a baby universe, or nonlocal encoding is required, and whether the question is even well-posed before a theory of quantum gravity is fixed.

My honest view is that the problem is underdetermined by the material I have here. I do not have the earlier commitment route, so I cannot say which of the competing resolutions the prior node was leaning toward, and I cannot check consistency against it. I can offer a structured way to place claims: options include (a) unitarity holds and information is encoded in subtle radiation correlations, (b) information is lost and quantum mechanics is modified, (c) information is stored in a remnant that never fully evaporates, or (d) the question requires a background-independent formulation in which 'the information' is not a conserved substance but a relational fact. The last option is often in the background of modern discussions but is rarely stated as a plain claim.

Given the missing prior, the most defensible contribution is to mark the gap rather than to fill it with an invented earlier position. The problem asks what happens to information; a fully satisfactory answer would need to specify the theory, the definition of information, the boundary conditions of the evaporation, and the operational sense in which the answer could be checked. Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Use FCL-1 for the commitment surface, encoded as a JSON document inside the commitments string: {"language":"FCL-1","records":[...],"uptake":[...]}. Each record has unique local id, type (claim|commitment|objection|use|problem), and text (unrestricted prose). Optional prose fields: scope, action, consequence, grounds, bearing. Optional arrays of references: target, depends, mentions, revises, withdraws. References are local IDs or exposed-artifact-label#local-ID; do not invent hidden IDs. A commitment proposes a scoped use, action, application or consequence; an objection alleges a defect whose bearing can itself be criticized; a use proposes an uptake or response; a problem states an unresolved question. depends asserts reliance; mentions only locates material. uptake lists the records you currently propose to use, not certified truths. No record type or optional field must be present. Empty records and uptake are allowed. Express uncertainty or an unrepresentable relation in prose rather than inventing a relation. The body remains unrestricted prose.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

# commitment_route

Develop an account of the problem using the available commitment surface. An earlier body, if any, is not supplied to this node. Express uncertainty caused by the view you actually have.
